subsection: 2. A Peripheral Irish Region: the West of Ireland

notes.h: Location and definition of the region
notes.b: This case study uses the West Region, made up of Counties Galway (including Galway city), Mayo and Roscommon. It is a peripheral region, meaning it lies far from the country's economic core around Dublin and from European markets.
points: Galway and Mayo lie on the Atlantic coast, so they face the ocean that shapes the region's weather, while Roscommon is inland.
Galway city is the region's only city, so it dominates the region's services and jobs, and Castlebar is the largest town in Mayo.
The three counties together form the State's West regional unit for statistics, so this is the standard definition of the region to use throughout.
notes.tip: Define the region once as Galway, Mayo and Roscommon and stick to it. The Western Development Commission's seven-county area is wider, so don't mix its facts in.

notes.b: A region is peripheral when several disadvantages add up and keep it behind the core. In the West they reinforce each other: distance and a harsh physical environment lead to a weak economy, and that drives people away.
points: Remote location: long distances to Dublin and to European markets raise transport costs for goods.
Difficult physical conditions: high rainfall, poor soils and rugged relief (the shape and height of the land) limit farming and building.
The population is small, scattered and ageing, after a long history of out-migration (people leaving the region) since the Great Famine of the late 1840s.
The economy depends on primary activities (farming, forestry, fishing) and the public sector, with lower incomes than the core.

Infrastructure (roads, rail, broadband) is weaker than in the core, with Galway city as the main exception, because it is a growth centre (a place planned and chosen to attract investment and population).
notes.tip: If asked to name a peripheral region and explain why it is peripheral, give the West and then these reasons: remote location, difficult physical conditions, a small ageing population, lower incomes and weaker infrastructure.

notes.b: A sketch map of the region is set as a question. Build it in layers: the outline first, then water, then towns, then relief (upland and lowland).
points: Outline Galway, Mayo and Roscommon, with the Atlantic coast along the western edge of Galway and Mayo.
Draw the River Corrib flowing from Lough Corrib through Galway city to Galway Bay.
Draw the River Moy reaching Killala Bay at Ballina, and the River Shannon along Roscommon's eastern edge.
Mark the urban centres, such as Galway city, Castlebar, Westport and Ballina.
Mark one upland: the Twelve Bens in Connemara, or Mweelrea in west Mayo.
Shade the limestone lowland (low, flat to rolling land on limestone rock) of east Galway and Roscommon.
Mark the Aran Islands offshore from Galway, for example as a small group of islands in the Atlantic.
notes.tip: Sketch map questions ask for the outline of the region, one river, one or two urban centres and one relief feature (an upland or a lowland).

notes.b: The West faces the Atlantic Ocean, which controls its weather. Moist, mild air arrives from the south-west and meets the western mountains, so the region is wet, windy, mild and cloudy.
points: The climate is cool temperate oceanic (mild and wet all year, with no extremes), strongly influenced by the Atlantic Ocean.
Prevailing south-westerly winds (the winds that blow most often) bring frequent depressions (low-pressure weather systems that bring rain and wind) and gales from the Atlantic.
Relief rainfall: moist Atlantic air is forced up over the western mountains, where it cools and drops its rain.
Annual rainfall is about 1,000 to 1,250 mm on lowlands and over 2,000 mm on some mountains, against about 750 to 1,000 mm in the east.
Winters are mild: mean January temperatures are about 4 to 7 °C, warmed by the North Atlantic Drift (a warm ocean current), so frost and snow are rare at the coast.
Summers are cool: mean July temperatures are about 14 to 16 °C, so the annual temperature range (the gap between winter and summer) is small.
The west is cloudier and less sunny than the east, because the moist Atlantic air arrives there first.
notes.tip: A short question may ask why the west is wetter and cloudier than the east. Answer with Atlantic air, south-westerly winds and relief rainfall over the western mountains.

notes.b: The wet, windy climate shapes what the land can be used for. It suits grass but works against almost everything else.
points: Grass grows well, but waterlogged land and wet weather make tillage (growing crops) difficult and hay hard to save, because it needs dry spells to dry.
Exposure to Atlantic gales limits the land that can be farmed and the crops that can be grown.
Gales and storms damage forests and power lines, because both stand exposed to the wind.
For example, Storm Éowyn, January 2025, caused widespread damage and power cuts across the West.
notes.tip: Climate is a physical factor for agriculture. Link it to grass growth, tillage and exposure rather than listing weather facts alone.

notes.b: Relief (the shape and height of the land) divides the West in two: rugged, hard-rock uplands in the west and low limestone land in the east. Between them lies an ice-scoured lowland, and the coast is cut up by the sea.
points: Rugged uplands in the west: the Twelve Bens and Maumturks in Connemara, and Mweelrea, Nephin and Croagh Patrick in Co. Mayo.
Mweelrea, 814 m, is the highest peak in Connacht (the province containing the West), so it is the tallest of these; Nephin is 806 m and Croagh Patrick is 764 m.
These are hard rocks, which resist erosion and so form the high ground: quartzite forms the Twelve Bens and Croagh Patrick; granite and mica schist form the uplands of Connemara.
The ice-scoured Connemara lowland has bare rock and many small lakes, because glaciers scraped away the soil and left hollows.
A low, flat to rolling limestone lowland lies in east Galway and Roscommon; Lough Corrib roughly divides it from the Connemara uplands.
Clew Bay's drowned drumlins are glacial hills (low hills of glacial deposit) that the sea now covers in part.
The Atlantic coast is heavily indented (cut by many inlets): Killary Harbour, a fjord (a long narrow inlet carved by a glacier) on the Galway–Mayo border, Clew Bay, and Achill Island.
Achill Island is the largest island off the Irish coast, so it is the biggest of Ireland's offshore islands; the Aran Islands are Carboniferous limestone, a continuation of the Burren limestone.
notes.tip: Croagh Patrick is quartzite, not limestone or granite, and the Aran Islands are limestone, not granite. Mweelrea (814 m), not Croagh Patrick, is the highest peak in Connacht.

notes.b: Soils follow relief and rainfall. Wet, steep, acidic ground gives poor soils in the west, and only the limestone lowland in the east has good ones. This is why most of the region suits only grazing.
points: Blanket bog (peat, a thick wet layer of partly rotted plants) covers much of west Mayo, around Bellacorick, and Connemara, where high rainfall keeps the ground waterlogged.
Leached, acidic podzols (soils with nutrients washed out of the top layer) with an iron pan (a hard, iron-rich layer) lie on the uplands.
Heavy, poorly drained gley soils (sticky, waterlogged clay soils) lie on the drumlins and clay lowlands.
Better-drained, more fertile brown earths lie on the limestone of east Galway and Roscommon.
Thin, rocky soils cover the limestone pavement (bare, flat limestone rock) of the Aran Islands, where islanders made soil from layers of sand and seaweed on bare rock.
notes.tip: Physical factors for agriculture include soils. Say which soil lies where and what each allows: peat, podzol and gley restrict farming, while brown earths on the limestone are the best.

notes.b: Drainage means how water leaves the land through rivers, lakes and underground. In the West, limestone sends some water underground, while poor natural drainage elsewhere leaves land liable to flood.
points: The River Corrib flows only a few kilometres from Lough Corrib through Galway city to Galway Bay.
Lough Corrib is the largest lake in the Republic of Ireland, so it is a major feature of the drainage.
Lough Mask's water flows underground to Lough Corrib near Cong, through the Cong 'dry canal', because limestone lets water drain through it.
Turloughs, seasonal lakes on limestone, such as Rahasane turlough near Craughwell, Co. Galway, flood in winter and drain away underground.
The River Moy reaches Killala Bay at Ballina, so Ballina lies on the river near its mouth.
The River Shannon and Lough Ree form much of Roscommon's eastern boundary; the River Suck flows through Ballinasloe to the Shannon.
Poor natural drainage leaves low land beside the Shannon liable to flooding.
The Moy arterial drainage scheme (deepening and straightening a river), run by the Office of Public Works under the Arterial Drainage Act 1945, was built to reduce flooding on the Moy.
notes.tip: Lough Corrib is the largest lake in the Republic, not in Ireland as a whole, because Lough Neagh in Northern Ireland is larger. Don't give lengths for the Corrib or Moy.

notes.b: Physical factors give the West a short effective grazing season (the part of the year when grass can actually be grazed) and restrict farming to grazing on most of the land.
points: High rainfall, waterlogged and leached soils, steep uplands and exposure give a short effective grazing season.
Tillage is restricted to the better-drained limestone soils of east Galway and Roscommon, because crops need drained soil.
Brown earths on the limestone of east Galway and Roscommon are the region's most fertile farmland, so this is where the best farming is.
Blanket bog and gley soils restrict most of the rest of the region to grazing, because they are too wet and poorly drained for crops.
notes.tip: Questions ask for physical factors influencing agriculture, such as climate, relief, soils and drainage, and for agriculture in two contrasting regions. The West gives the difficult half of the contrast.

notes.b: Human and economic factors add to the physical limits. Farms are small, incomes are low and the region is far from the buyers of its produce.
points: Farms are small and often fragmented (split into several separate plots), a legacy of the pre-Famine rundale system (shared land held in scattered strips) and of population pressure on the land.
The Congested Districts Board, set up in 1891, improved conditions in the poor western districts through land consolidation (joining scattered plots), piers and cottage industries.
The Land Commission later consolidated holdings, which reduced fragmentation further.
Part-time farming, with off-farm jobs supplementing low farm incomes, because farm income alone is not enough.
Income depends heavily on subsidies and EU payments, which come from the EU's Common Agricultural Policy (CAP).
Distance from markets and ports adds to the cost of moving livestock and produce.
notes.tip: For agriculture with any two factors, markets are one option: distance from markets and ports is the West's economic disadvantage.

notes.b: Because most of the land suits only grass, the West's farming is based on animals, mainly cattle and sheep.
points: Cattle rearing is the main enterprise: suckler herds (cows that rear their own calves) rear calves, and young store cattle (young animals not yet ready for slaughter) are sold through local marts (livestock markets) to farmers in the east to be fattened.
Sheep graze the hill commonage (shared hill land) of Connemara and the Mayo mountains.
There is little tillage or dairying compared with the south and east, because the wet, poorly drained land is poorly suited to both.
The October Fair at Ballinasloe, Co. Galway, is one of Europe's oldest horse fairs, an example of the West's animal-based farming.
The Connemara pony is Ireland's native pony breed, another example of the region's livestock.

notes.b: Low farm incomes and the pressure of subsidy-driven sheep farming brought two kinds of problem: people leaving the land and damage to the hills. Schemes then tried to put these right.
points: Low incomes, ageing farmers and few young successors lead to land abandonment, because no one is left to work the farm.
CAP headage payments (payments per animal kept) from the 1980s raised sheep numbers on the hill commonage of Connemara and the Mayo mountains.
Overgrazing stripped vegetation from the hills and eroded the peat.
The Rural Environment Protection Scheme (REPS), from 1994, was a response to the damage.
Commonage Framework Plans, from the early 2000s, set out how shared hill land is to be managed.
Area-based payments paid farmers on the area of land they farm, not per animal, so there was no reward for keeping more sheep.
Diversification (adding new income sources) into agri-tourism and forestry.
notes.tip: A question on problems and responses expects both: the problem (low income, ageing farmers, land abandonment or overgrazing) and the response (REPS, area-based payments or diversification).

notes.b: Forestry is a primary activity (using natural resources) that suits land too poor for farming. Trees can be grown on wet, acidic ground where grazing pays badly.
points: Conifer plantations, mainly Sitka spruce (native to western North America), cover marginal land (poor land where farming barely pays) and blanket bog where farming pays poorly.
Coillte, founded in 1988, is the State forestry company, so it is the main planter and manager of State forests.
Planting grants and premiums (payments to landowners) encourage forestry on farmland and bog.
Benefits: income from timber, jobs, and carbon storage in the trees.
Forest cover in Ireland is about 11% (2020s), which is low, so there is room for more planting.
notes.tip: For two factors influencing a primary activity such as forestry, use the marginal land and blanket bog, and the grants and premiums.

notes.b: Forestry on this scale has costs for water, landscape and the stability of the ground.
points: Acidification of streams from conifer plantations, which harms the water for fish.
Monoculture (one species grown over a large area) and landscape impact of large blocks of single-species forest.
Peat slide (a mass of wet peat slipping downhill) at Derrybrien, Slieve Aughty Mountains, Co. Galway, on 16 October 2003: about 450,000 m³ of peat slid during wind-farm construction on forested bog.
The EU Court of Justice fined Ireland in 2019 over Derrybrien, so the slide had legal consequences.
notes.tip: Name Derrybrien with its date and the 450,000 m³ figure as your example of a peat slide on forested bog.

notes.b: The Atlantic coast and the inland lakes and rivers give the West fishing, fish farming (aquaculture), seaweed harvesting and angling (fishing with rod and line). The sheltered bays are used for farming the sea.
points: Rossaveel, Co. Galway, is one of six State Fishery Harbour Centres (State-supported fishing ports) and the ferry port for the Aran Islands.
Killary Harbour: rope-grown mussels are farmed on mussel rafts.
Salmon farms in Connemara bays raise concerns over sea lice (parasites on the fish) and pollution.
Seaweed, a resource of the shore, is harvested and processed by Arramara Teoranta at Kilkieran, Connemara.
Angling: salmon on the River Moy at Ballina, including the Ridge Pool, and brown trout on Lough Corrib and Lough Mask.
Problems: EU fishing quotas (limits on the catch), loss of quota after Brexit (the UK's departure from the EU), small boats and distance from markets.
notes.tip: Killybegs is in Co. Donegal, outside this region. Use Rossaveel as the West's fishing port.

notes.b: Bellacorick shows the West's energy changing from peat to wind. The region's exposure to the Atlantic, a problem for farming, is an advantage for renewable energy.
points: Bellacorick, Co. Mayo, had a peat-fired power station, which closed in 2003.
Bellacorick wind farm (1992) was Ireland's first commercial wind farm, so it began wind energy in the same place as the peat station.
The Oweninny wind farm is on cutaway bog (bog where the peat has been removed) nearby, so worked-out land is reused for energy.
Strong Atlantic winds and waves give the region high renewable energy potential.
The Atlantic Marine Energy Test Site off Belmullet, Co. Mayo, tests wave energy.

notes.b: The West has had gas, coal, marble and gold. Some projects went ahead, one caused conflict and one was refused.
points: The Corrib gas field, off north-west Mayo, was discovered in 1996.
Gas first flowed in December 2015, many years after discovery; gas is processed at the Bellanaboy terminal.
The Shell to Sea campaign opposed the project, for example through protest, and the 'Rossport Five' were jailed in 2005.
Arigna, Co. Roscommon: coal mining ended in 1990; the site is now the Arigna Mining Experience, a visitor attraction.
Connemara marble is quarried, using the region's hard metamorphic rock.
Croagh Patrick: gold was found in the 1980s, but mining was not allowed after public opposition.

notes.b: Manufacturing (making goods in factories) is a secondary activity. In the West it is thin and clustered in a few places, which reflects the region's peripheral position.
points: Manufacturing is limited and concentrated in Galway city and a few towns: Castlebar, Westport and Ballina.
There are few heavy industries, so most rural areas have little manufacturing.
Small food-processing and craft firms are the main rural manufacturers, for example firms using local produce.
notes.tip: Questions on a secondary activity ask for the pattern and then the factors behind it. Start with where manufacturing is found: Galway city, Castlebar, Westport and Ballina.

notes.h: Case study: the Galway medical devices cluster
notes.b: A cluster is a group of related firms in one place that support each other. Galway's medical-technology cluster grew from a factory closure that left skilled workers looking for jobs.
points: Digital Equipment Corporation (DEC) closed its Galway manufacturing plant in 1993, leaving a skilled workforce.
Boston Scientific opened in Galway in 1994, and Medtronic followed at Parkmore.
Suppliers and start-ups clustered around the multinationals (large firms that operate in many countries), with links to the University of Galway.
Galway is now one of Europe's leading medical-technology clusters.
notes.tip: Give no medtech job numbers, as none are checked.

notes.b: Mayo has no large city, but several multinationals have set up in its towns. Each is a named example of foreign investment in the West.
points: For example, Baxter Healthcare, Castlebar.
Allergan, now part of AbbVie, Westport, which makes Botox, a medical product.
Hollister, Ballina, which spreads manufacturing beyond Galway.
Coca-Cola concentrate plant, Ballina, an example of a multinational that does not make medical products.

notes.b: State and EU policy tries to steer industry towards the peripheral West with grants, designated centres and agencies. Exams ask for any two factors, and this is one of the five.
points: IDA Ireland (the State agency that attracts foreign firms) and regional incentives attract foreign manufacturing firms to the region.
Údarás na Gaeltachta, set up in 1980 with its head office at Na Forbacha, Co. Galway, gives grants to firms in Gaeltacht areas (the Irish-speaking districts).
The National Spatial Strategy (2002) named Galway a gateway (a major centre intended to drive regional growth) and Castlebar–Ballina a linked hub (a smaller centre working together as one unit).
The National Planning Framework (Project Ireland 2040), 2018, requires Galway, Cork, Limerick and Waterford each to grow by at least 50% by 2040.
The Western Development Commission, a statutory body (set up by law) under the Western Development Commission Act 1998, promotes development in the west.
notes.tip: Secondary activity questions ask for two factors from government policy, labour, markets, infrastructure and raw materials. Develop each factor with named examples.

notes.b: Firms locate where they can find skilled workers. Galway has a supply, but the rest of the region loses its skilled young people.
points: The University of Galway, founded in 1845 as Queen's College Galway and given its present name in 2022, supplies graduates, so firms can recruit trained staff locally.
Atlantic Technological University (ATU), with campuses in Galway and Mayo, supplies graduates and skilled workers, so firms in both counties can recruit trained staff.
Outside Galway, the pool of skilled workers is small, because skilled young people leave the region.

notes.b: A market is where the firm's customers are. The West's market is small and far from its largest buyers.
points: The local market is small and scattered, with low population density across much of the region, so few customers live near any one factory.
Galway city provides the largest local market, because it is the biggest concentration of people in the region.
Exports must travel long distances to ports and airports, which raises costs.

notes.b: Infrastructure (roads, rail, broadband) lets firms move goods and information, and raw materials are the inputs that factories use. Both vary across the region.
points: Good road links to Galway city, so firms there can move goods, but weaker roads and broadband in rural areas.
EU Structural Funds (EU money for poorer regions) have paid for roads and broadband.
Local farm and fish produce supplies the food-processing firms.
Medtech firms import the materials they use, so local raw materials matter less to them.

notes.b: The same peripheral position that limits the pattern of industry also creates problems for firms already in the West. Most of these come back to distance and small size.
points: Peripheral location adds to transport costs for goods, because firms ship over long distances.
The labour pool outside Galway city is small, so firms have fewer workers to choose from.
Dependence on a few multinationals, and closures such as DEC's in 1993, which show the risk when one large employer leaves.
Difficulty attracting investment away from Galway, so the rest of the region gets less of it.
Poor rural infrastructure, which makes it hard for firms to locate in rural towns.

notes.b: Tourism is a tertiary activity (a service). The West's main selling point is its Atlantic landscape of mountains, islands and coast.
points: Connemara National Park, at Letterfrack, protects the Connemara landscape, so visitors can see it unspoilt.
Killary Harbour, Croagh Patrick, Achill Island and Clew Bay draw visitors to the coast and mountains, because of their scenery.
For example, Dún Aonghasa, a prehistoric stone fort on a cliff edge on Inis Mór, Aran Islands.
The Atlantic coast and beaches are used for surfing and water sports.
The Wild Atlantic Way, a Fáilte Ireland touring route launched in 2014, runs about 2,500 km from Inishowen, Co. Donegal, to Kinsale, Co. Cork.
notes.tip: Ordinary Level questions ask for the region's advantages for an activity. For tourism, the landscape, the culture and the Wild Atlantic Way are all advantages. Give no visitor numbers.

notes.b: Culture and history give visitors reasons to come beyond the scenery. They include language, ancient sites, historic houses and festivals.
points: Gaeltacht culture and the Irish language, with Irish summer colleges, which attract students to the Gaeltacht.
Céide Fields, north Co. Mayo: Stone Age (Neolithic) field systems over 5,000 years old, preserved under blanket bog.
Kylemore Abbey, Connemara, a Benedictine abbey, is a heritage attraction.
Westport House, a historic house, is a heritage attraction.
Strokestown Park and the National Famine Museum, Co. Roscommon.
Rathcroghan, Co. Roscommon: the ancient royal site of Connacht, which draws visitors interested in early history.
Lough Key Forest Park, near Boyle, offers outdoor recreation.
Galway International Arts Festival (July); Galway was European Capital of Culture in 2020, a year disrupted by COVID-19.

notes.b: Active holidays and events make use of the landscape and of Galway city.
points: Angling, walking and cycling, which use the region's rivers, lakes and countryside.
For example, the Great Western Greenway, about 42 km from Westport to Achill, first opened in 2010.
Galway city's festivals, nightlife and the Galway Races at Ballybrit in summer.

notes.b: Tourism brings income, but it has weaknesses that come from the West's weather, distance and size.
points: The season is short and depends on the weather, because most visitors come in good weather.
Seasonal and low-paid jobs, because tourism work is only available for part of the year.
Distance and weaker access than the east, which make the journey harder for visitors.
Pressure on fragile landscapes and on the Irish language, because large numbers of visitors wear the land and bring English into Gaeltacht areas.
Over-reliance on Galway city, so the rest of the region gains less.
notes.tip: For an Ordinary Level challenge, seasonality is the example the package gives, so explain it: a short season that depends on the weather.

notes.b: Better transport reduces the effects of distance. The West has gained motorways, an airport and rail links, though not every link is open.
points: M6 Dublin–Galway motorway, completed in 2009, which shortens the journey to the capital.
M17/M18 Galway–Tuam motorway, 2017, which links Galway with Tuam.
Ireland West Airport Knock opened in 1986, promoted by Monsignor James Horan, and it gives air access to the north of the region.
Rail lines run from Galway, Westport and Ballina to Dublin, which link the main towns to the capital.
The Western Rail Corridor's Ennis–Athenry section reopened in 2010; the line north of Athenry to Claremorris has not reopened.
Ferries link the islands to the mainland, because the islands have no road link.
notes.tip: Use Ireland West Airport Knock, not Galway Airport, which has no checked current status. Don't say the Western Rail Corridor is open north of Athenry.

notes.b: Even with improvements, transport in the West has weaknesses that come from its thin population. Good transport still matters for the region's economy.
points: Low population density makes public transport uneconomic outside the towns, because there are too few passengers.
Poor minor roads and heavy dependence on the car, because buses and trains are too few.
Congestion in Galway city: the Galway City Ring Road has been proposed for many years but not built.
Long journey times to Dublin, which adds to peripherality.
Transport supports tourism and industry and reduces peripherality.
notes.tip: Questions on tourism or transport ask for factors. Give improvements and problems, then say that transport supports tourism and industry and reduces peripherality.

notes.b: Services besides tourism and transport also provide jobs, and most are based in Galway city.
points: A major hospital in Galway city serves as a regional centre for the west, so patients from the three counties travel there.
Public-sector jobs, including decentralised government offices (offices moved out of Dublin).

notes.b: Galway is the West's only city and the urban area to use for a question on one urban area. Its location where a river meets the sea explains why it began.
points: Galway city lies where the River Corrib reaches Galway Bay.
It began as an Anglo-Norman walled town, from the 13th century, so the walls protected the settlement.
The Spanish Arch recalls medieval trade with Spain, so it shows Galway's past as a trading port.
'City of the Tribes' is the city's name for the 14 merchant families who ran its trade.
Eyre Square is the city's central open space, so it is a landmark of the city centre.
notes.tip: Questions on factors influencing one urban area expect Galway city, so use its site, history, university, industry and planning status.

notes.b: Galway has grown into the region's centre for education, industry, health and planning. Growth has also brought urban problems.
points: Galway city had about 85,000 people in the Galway City Council area in Census 2022.
The University of Galway has been in the city since 1845, which gives the city graduates and research.
Galway is a designated growth centre in national planning policy, named a gateway in 2002 and set to grow by at least 50% by 2040 under the National Planning Framework.
Galway is a medical-technology cluster, which shows its industrial growth since DEC and the medtech firms.
For example, Oranmore is a growing satellite town (a smaller settlement near a city that takes some of its growth).
Suburban sprawl (the spread of housing over the edge of the city) and housing costs in the growing city.
Traffic congestion, because the Galway City Ring Road is still not built.

notes.b: Beyond Galway, the West's towns are small. They serve local areas rather than forming a strong network of larger towns.
points: Castlebar is the county town of Mayo, so it is the administrative centre of the county.
Westport is an 18th-century planned town laid out for the Browne family of Westport House.
Westport's Octagon and the Mall, along the Carrowbeg River, show its planned layout.
Ballina lies on the River Moy; Tuam is the seat of the Catholic Archdiocese of Tuam.
Ballinasloe, Co. Galway, and Boyle, near Lough Key Forest Park, are small towns, for example serving their local areas.
The towns form a weak urban hierarchy (the ranking of settlements by size and services): few large towns and no large city beyond Galway.

notes.b: The West has a small share of the State's people, and they are spread very unevenly. Exams ask you to account for the distribution, which means explaining each pattern with a reason.
points: The region had about 486,000 people in Census 2022, about 9% of the State's 5.1 million.
Galway (including Galway city) about 278,000, Mayo about 138,000 and Roscommon about 70,000 in Census 2022.
Mayo has about 25 people per km² (area about 5,590 km², Ireland's third-largest county); Roscommon has under 30 per km².
The State average is about 73 per km², and Co. Dublin has about 1,600 per km², which shows how thinly the West is settled.
Concentration in Galway city and its suburbs and satellite towns, where jobs, services and transport are.
Moderate densities on the east Galway, Roscommon and east Mayo lowlands and in the towns, where land and roads are better.
Very low densities on the uplands and blanket bogs of west Mayo (Erris) and Connemara, where soils are poor, slopes steep and the land exposed.
Coastal and island settlement, linked to fishing and the Gaeltacht, as on the Aran Islands.
notes.tip: To account for the distribution, give each pattern with its reason: Galway city for jobs, services and transport; the lowlands for better land and roads; the uplands and bogs for poor soils, steep slopes and exposure.

notes.b: Population dynamics means how a population changes over time. The West's history of loss is now partly reversed in places.
points: The Great Famine of the late 1840s hit the West hard, because many people depended on small farms.
A long history of emigration has left populations far below pre-Famine levels, so the West has not recovered its earlier numbers.
Continuing out-migration of young adults to Dublin and abroad, known as brain drain (the loss of educated, skilled people).
An ageing population with fewer births and many empty houses, because the young have left.
Recent growth from return migration (emigrants coming home), immigration and the expansion of Galway city.
The population of every county grew between 2016 and 2022 (Census 2022).
notes.tip: Describe population change without emigration numbers, birth rates or historic county figures, as none are checked.

notes.b: Rural settlement in the West has changed from old clustered and scattered forms to housing strung along roads. Rural life has also declined as people have left.
points: Traditional dispersed settlement (houses spread out across the land) and clachans, small clusters of houses shared by families under rundale.
Later ribbon development (houses in a line along roads) and one-off housing, because roads give access to services.
Rural decline, which follows from out-migration: depopulation, an ageing population, and closures of schools, post offices and Garda stations.
Island depopulation, especially on the Aran Islands, where fewer people stay.

notes.b: Governments and the EU have launched programmes to support rural areas. Some invest in places that have lost population and some bring in jobs and services.
points: CLÁR programme (2001): investment in depopulated rural areas, to slow the decline.
LEADER, the EU rural development programme, which funds local projects.
National Broadband Plan: contract signed in 2019 with National Broadband Ireland, to bring broadband to rural areas.
Our Rural Future (2021): rural development policy.
Remote-working hubs and digital hubs bring work to rural towns, so people can work there without commuting to the city.
The Western Development Commission covers seven counties, including Galway, Mayo and Roscommon, which is wider than the three-county region used here.
The Congested Districts Board of 1891 was an earlier response, and Údarás na Gaeltachta supports Gaeltacht areas by giving grants to firms.

notes.b: The West holds Ireland's largest Gaeltacht areas, the districts where Irish is the main community language.
points: The Galway Gaeltacht is the largest; it includes Connemara and the Aran Islands.
The Mayo Gaeltacht: Erris (Iorras), Achill (Acaill) and Tourmakeady (Tuar Mhic Éadaigh).
Roscommon has no Gaeltacht area, so Irish-speaking districts lie only in Galway and Mayo.
The Census 2022 Gaeltacht population was about 106,000.

notes.h: Language: the decline of daily speakers
notes.b: Fewer people now use Irish every day, even inside the Gaeltacht. Several forces push the language back.
points: About 20,000 people speak Irish daily outside the education system in the Gaeltacht; about 72,000 do so nationally (Census 2022).
Emigration of young speakers from the Gaeltacht, which removes the next generation of speakers.
English-language media and English spoken in the home, which reduce daily use of Irish.
Tourism and the in-migration of English speakers into Gaeltacht areas, which makes English the common language locally.
notes.tip: Don't copy daily-speaker counts for individual Gaeltacht areas. Use the Census 2022 figures here.

notes.b: Institutions and strategies try to protect Irish in the Gaeltacht. They include State bodies, media, laws and plans, schooling and housing.
points: Údarás na Gaeltachta (1980), head office at Na Forbacha, Co. Galway, is the State body responsible for the Gaeltacht's development.
TG4, launched in 1996 as Teilifís na Gaeilge, with its headquarters at Baile na hAbhann, Co. Galway.
RTÉ Raidió na Gaeltachta, from 1972, with its headquarters at Casla (Costelloe), Co. Galway.
Gaeltacht Act 2012: language-planning areas.
20-Year Strategy for the Irish Language, 2010–2030.
Irish-medium schools (where lessons are taught in Irish) and summer colleges, so young people use Irish regularly.
Planning conditions that reserve new houses for Irish speakers, so that new housing goes to Irish speakers.
Údarás jobs to keep young people in the Gaeltacht, which counters emigration.
notes.tip: A question may ask for one strategy to address the decline in daily Irish speakers. Language planning under the Gaeltacht Act 2012, Údarás jobs, Irish-medium education and summer colleges, housing conditions, and TG4 and Raidió na Gaeltachta all fit.

notes.b: The West is strongly Roman Catholic, and its religion shows in pilgrimage sites and old church centres. Religion also draws tourists.
points: The West has a higher Roman Catholic share than Dublin; nationally, about 69% of people are Roman Catholic and about 14% have no religion (Census 2022).
For example, Knock Shrine, Co. Mayo: an apparition was reported in 1879; Pope John Paul II visited in 1979 and Pope Francis in 2018.
Croagh Patrick pilgrimage on Reek Sunday, the last Sunday in July, for example, draws pilgrims to the mountain.
Ballintubber Abbey, Co. Mayo, was founded in 1216, and Mass has been celebrated there continuously since.
Tuam is the seat of the Catholic Archdiocese of Tuam, so it is a church centre for the region.
Religious practice and vocations (people entering the priesthood) are declining, but religion remains important in community life.
notes.tip: Give no regional percentage for Catholics. Say only that the West's share is higher than Dublin's, and use the national Census 2022 figures.

keyTerms.definition: A region far from the main centres of population and economic activity, with poorer access and fewer opportunities.
A thick layer of peat that covers the land where high rainfall keeps the ground waterlogged.
An acidic, leached soil in which minerals wash down from the surface layer, often leaving a hard iron pan below.
A grey, poorly drained soil that stays waterlogged for much of the year.
A smooth, oval hill of glacial material shaped by moving ice.
A seasonal lake in limestone country that fills with water in winter and drains away underground in summer.
A traditional system in which families shared scattered strips of land within a townland.
A small, traditional cluster of houses in which families shared land.
Unfenced hill land shared by several farmers for grazing.
A grant paid per animal, which encouraged farmers to keep more livestock.
A herd of cows kept to rear calves for sale.
Young cattle sold to other farmers to be fattened.
An area where Irish is the main language of daily life in the community.
The emigration of skilled, educated young people from an area.
The design and manufacture of medical devices and equipment.

factCards.term: West of Ireland (Galway, Mayo, Roscommon): why it is a peripheral region
factCards.definition: Remote from Dublin and European markets; high rainfall, poor soils, rugged relief; a small, scattered, ageing population after long out-migration; dependence on primary activities and the public sector; weaker infrastructure. Galway city is the exception.

factCards.term: West of Ireland sketch map: what to draw
factCards.definition: The outline of Galway, Mayo and Roscommon; the River Corrib (or the Moy, or the Shannon on the eastern edge); Galway city and Castlebar; an upland such as the Twelve Bens, Croagh Patrick or Mweelrea; the limestone lowland of east Galway and Roscommon.

factCards.term: West of Ireland climate: why it is so wet and windy
factCards.definition: Prevailing south-westerlies bring Atlantic depressions and relief rain on western mountains: about 1,000–1,250 mm a year on lowlands, over 2,000 mm on some mountains. The North Atlantic Drift keeps winters mild; frequent gales (Storm Éowyn, January 2025).

factCards.term: West of Ireland relief: named uplands and their rocks
factCards.definition: Mweelrea (814 m), Connacht's highest peak; Nephin (806 m); Croagh Patrick (764 m, quartzite); the quartzite Twelve Bens and the Maumturks in Connemara, with marble and mica schist. East Galway and Roscommon are low limestone lowland.

factCards.term: West of Ireland soils: types and where they are found
factCards.definition: Blanket bog over much of west Mayo (Erris, Bellacorick) and Connemara; acidic, leached podzols on uplands; poorly drained gleys on drumlins; better brown earths on limestone in east Galway and Roscommon; Aran Islands soil made from sand and seaweed.

factCards.term: West of Ireland drainage: named lakes, rivers and turloughs
factCards.definition: The short Corrib flows from Lough Corrib, the Republic's largest lake, through Galway to the sea; Lough Mask drains underground to Lough Corrib near Cong; Rahasane turlough; the Moy reaches Killala Bay at Ballina; the Shannon and Lough Ree edge Roscommon.

factCards.term: West of Ireland agriculture: physical factors that limit it
factCards.definition: Heavy rain waterlogs the land, making tillage and hay saving difficult; leached, acidic soils, steep uplands and exposure shorten the effective grazing season, so most land suits only grazing. Better land lies on the limestone of east Galway and Roscommon.

factCards.term: West of Ireland agriculture: farm structure, problems and responses
factCards.definition: Small, fragmented farms, a rundale legacy, partly consolidated by the Congested Districts Board (1891); older farmers, low incomes, part-time farming, reliance on CAP; overgrazed commonage after 1980s headage payments. Responses: REPS (1994), diversification.

factCards.term: West of Ireland farm types
factCards.definition: Cattle rearing with suckler herds, selling store cattle at local marts to eastern farmers for fattening; sheep on hill commonage in Connemara and Mayo; little tillage or dairying; Connemara ponies; the Ballinasloe October Fair, an ancient horse fair.

factCards.term: Fishing and aquaculture in the West: named places
factCards.definition: Rossaveel: a State Fishery Harbour Centre and the Aran Islands ferry port. Rope-grown mussels in Killary Harbour; salmon farms in Connemara bays; seaweed processing at Kilkieran (Arramara Teoranta); salmon angling on the Moy at Ballina.

factCards.term: Corrib gas field: key facts
factCards.definition: Off north-west Mayo: discovered in 1996; gas first flowed in December 2015 to the Bellanaboy terminal. The 'Shell to Sea' campaign opposed it, and the 'Rossport Five' were jailed in 2005.

factCards.term: Energy in the West: from peat to wind and waves
factCards.definition: Bellacorick's peat-fired station closed in 2003; Bellacorick wind farm (1992) was Ireland's first commercial wind farm, and Oweninny wind farm is on nearby cutaway bog. The Atlantic Marine Energy Test Site off Belmullet tests wave energy.

factCards.term: Galway medical devices cluster: how it developed
factCards.definition: Digital Equipment Corporation closed its Galway plant in 1993, leaving skilled workers; Boston Scientific opened in 1994, then Medtronic (Parkmore); suppliers and start-ups clustered, linked to the University of Galway: now a leading European medtech cluster.

factCards.term: Manufacturing outside Galway city: name four Mayo multinationals
factCards.definition: Outside Galway city, manufacturing is limited to a few towns: Baxter Healthcare, Castlebar; Allergan (now part of AbbVie), Westport, making Botox; Hollister, Ballina; Coca-Cola concentrate plant, Ballina.

factCards.term: West of Ireland manufacturing: government policy as a factor
factCards.definition: IDA Ireland; Údarás na Gaeltachta grants; EU Structural Funds for roads and broadband; the Western Development Commission (1998); Galway a gateway in the National Spatial Strategy (2002), to grow at least 50% by 2040 (National Planning Framework, 2018).

factCards.term: West of Ireland manufacturing: problems
factCards.definition: Peripheral location and high transport costs; small, scattered markets; a small labour pool outside Galway and out-migration of skilled young people; dependence on a few multinationals; closures such as DEC; poor rural infrastructure.

factCards.term: West of Ireland tourism: landscape attractions and routes
factCards.definition: Connemara National Park (Letterfrack), Killary Harbour fjord, Croagh Patrick, Achill Island, Clew Bay, Dún Aonghasa on Inis Mór; the Wild Atlantic Way (2014, about 2,500 km); the Great Western Greenway (about 42 km, Westport to Achill, 2010).

factCards.term: West of Ireland tourism: culture and heritage attractions
factCards.definition: Céide Fields (Neolithic fields over 5,000 years old under bog); Kylemore Abbey; Westport House; Strokestown Park and the National Famine Museum; Rathcroghan; Knock Shrine; Gaeltacht culture; Galway's Arts Festival, Races and 2020 European Capital of Culture.

factCards.term: West of Ireland transport: improvements, with dates
factCards.definition: M6 Dublin–Galway (2009); M17/M18 Galway–Tuam (2017); Ireland West Airport Knock (1986, promoted by Monsignor James Horan); rail to Dublin from Galway, Westport and Ballina; Western Rail Corridor reopened Ennis–Athenry (2010), but not north of Athenry.

factCards.term: West of Ireland population: Census 2022 figures and density
factCards.definition: About 486,000, about 9% of the State. Co. Galway including the city about 278,000 (Galway City Council area about 85,000); Mayo about 138,000; Roscommon about 70,000. Mayo has about 25 people per km², against a State average of about 73.

factCards.term: West of Ireland: account for the distribution of population
factCards.definition: Highest in Galway city and its suburbs (jobs, services, transport); moderate on the east Galway, Roscommon and east Mayo lowlands (better land, roads); very low on the uplands and bogs of west Mayo and Connemara (poor soils, steep slopes, exposure).

factCards.term: West of Ireland population dynamics
factCards.definition: The Great Famine (late 1840s) hit the West hardest; long emigration left populations far below pre-Famine levels. Young adults still leave (brain drain), so it is ageing, but every county grew 2016–2022 with return migration, immigration and Galway's growth.

factCards.term: Galway city: factors in its development, and its problems
factCards.definition: Lowest crossing of the Corrib on Galway Bay; 13th-century Anglo-Norman walled town; trading port, 'City of the Tribes' (14 merchant families), Spanish Arch; university since 1845; DEC then medtech. Problems: congestion, housing costs, no ring road.

factCards.term: Gaeltacht areas in the West, and why daily Irish speaking is declining
factCards.definition: Galway (Connemara, Cois Fharraige, the Aran Islands: the largest Gaeltacht) and Mayo (Erris, Achill, Tourmakeady); Roscommon has none. Decline: emigration, English-language media, tourism, in-migration of English speakers, English in the home.

factCards.term: Strategies to address the decline in daily Irish speakers in the Gaeltacht
factCards.definition: Language-planning areas under the Gaeltacht Act 2012; the 20-Year Strategy 2010–2030; Údarás na Gaeltachta jobs for young people; Irish-medium schools and summer colleges; housing reserved for Irish speakers; TG4 and Raidió na Gaeltachta.

factCards.term: Religion in the West: named sites and facts
factCards.definition: Higher Catholic share than Dublin. Knock Shrine: apparition reported 1879; papal visits 1979 and 2018. Croagh Patrick: Reek Sunday pilgrimage, last Sunday in July. Ballintubber Abbey (1216): Mass celebrated continuously. Tuam: Catholic archdiocese seat.

questions.prompt: Examine the physical factors that influence the development of agriculture in a peripheral Irish region you have studied.
questions.model: Climate: the West Region is cool and wet. Rainfall is about 1,000 to 1,250 mm on the lowlands and over 2,000 mm on some mountains, so the land is waterlogged and hay is hard to save. Mild winters, with January temperatures of about 4 to 7 °C warmed by the North Atlantic Drift, and cool summers, with July temperatures of about 14 to 16 °C, keep frost and snow rare at the coast. Exposure to Atlantic gales limits farming. Grass grows well, so farming is mainly cattle rearing and sheep grazing, with little tillage. Relief: the uplands of Connemara, including the Twelve Bens and Maumturks, and of west Mayo, including Mweelrea (814 m), Nephin (806 m) and Croagh Patrick (764 m), are too steep and exposed for anything but rough grazing. The flatter limestone lowlands of east Galway and Roscommon carry the better farms. Soils: blanket bog around Bellacorick and in Connemara is unsuited to farming; acidic podzols with an iron pan on the uplands support only rough grazing; poorly drained gley soils on the drumlins and clay lowlands support wet pasture; better-drained brown earths on the limestone of east Galway and Roscommon are the most fertile soils. Drainage: poor natural drainage leaves land beside the Shannon liable to flooding; turloughs such as Rahasane turlough, near Craughwell, Co. Galway, flood in winter and limit the use of the land; underground drainage through the limestone carries water from Lough Mask to Lough Corrib near Cong; the Moy arterial drainage scheme, run by the Office of Public Works, was built to reduce flooding on the Moy.

questions.prompt: Examine two factors that have influenced the development of tourism in a peripheral Irish region you have studied.
questions.model: Physical landscape: the Atlantic coast and mountains of Connemara and west Mayo draw visitors, including Killary Harbour, Clew Bay, Croagh Patrick and Achill Island, the largest island off the Irish coast. Dún Aonghasa, a prehistoric stone fort on a cliff edge on Inis Mór in the Aran Islands, adds to the scenery. The Atlantic beaches are used for surfing and water sports. Connemara National Park at Letterfrack protects the Connemara landscape. The Wild Atlantic Way, a Fáilte Ireland touring route launched in 2014 along about 2,500 km of coast from Inishowen, Co. Donegal, to Kinsale, Co. Cork, brings visitors along this scenery. Culture and heritage: the Gaeltacht culture and the Irish language, taught in summer colleges, attract visitors to Connemara and the Mayo Gaeltacht. Céide Fields in north Co. Mayo, Stone Age field systems over 5,000 years old preserved under blanket bog, attract visitors interested in archaeology. Kylemore Abbey, a Benedictine abbey in Connemara, draws visitors. Strokestown Park and the National Famine Museum in Co. Roscommon, and Rathcroghan, the ancient royal site of Connacht, add to the heritage offer. Knock Shrine, Co. Mayo, where an apparition was reported in 1879, and the Croagh Patrick pilgrimage on Reek Sunday attract religious visitors. Galway's Arts Festival and its year as European Capital of Culture in 2020, which was disrupted by COVID-19, drew cultural visitors to the city.

questions.prompt: Account for the distribution of population in a peripheral Irish region you have studied.
questions.model: The West Region had about 486,000 people in Census 2022, about 9% of the State's population, and its density is low. Population is most concentrated in Galway city and its suburbs and satellite towns such as Oranmore, where jobs, the university, the hospital, services and transport links are concentrated. Densities are moderate in the eastern lowlands of east Galway, Roscommon and east Mayo, and in the towns of Castlebar, Westport, Ballina, Tuam and Ballinasloe, where the land is better and roads and jobs are available. Densities are very low on the western uplands and blanket bogs of west Mayo, such as Erris, and on Connemara, where poor soils, steep slopes and exposure to Atlantic weather limit farming and settlement. Mayo has about 25 people per km² and Roscommon under 30 per km², against about 73 per km² for the State. Island settlement on the Aran Islands and the coastal Gaeltacht communities depend on fishing and the Irish language. Historically, the Great Famine of the late 1840s and a long history of emigration have left the West with a population far below pre-Famine levels, and continuing out-migration of young adults keeps numbers low.
